Line Price Price against it 200-day average $30.88 61.7% below 50-day average $27.08 56.3% below 21-day average $18.96 37.6% below Now $11.82 Last close $12.30 · Nov 16 why? ⓘ The 21-day average is the line the stock has hovered around for about a month. A "day's move" is the stock's ATR ($2.04 here), how far it normally travels in a day, and it is the same number your stop on the Trade Setup card uses. The gauge places the price and the 21, 50 and 200-day averages by how many day-moves they sit from the 21-day average, and the ladder under it gives their real prices. Closer to the 21-day line usually means a closer stop; well above it means buying after a run. The marks are a measuring stick for your own judgment, not signals, and STA has not tested them. Volume behind the move No volume data: the data source reports no shares traded on 50 of the last 50 days, so the volume checks are left out. What these numbers are The three tiles are common rules of thumb: at least 7 of 8 trend checks pass, RSI is between 50 and 70 (rising but not overheated), and the stock has done better than the S&P 500 over the past year. STA has not tested them, and they do not predict what happens next. They describe the stock; the decision is yours. Why only 4 checks are listed: the full score uses 8 checks from Mark Minervini's Trend Template. The 4 listed are the ones most traders lean on; the other 4 mostly repeat them. Trend strength (ADX): ADX measures how hard the price is pushing in one direction. Below 20 means it's moving sideways right now. In an uptrend that usually means resting, not a broken trend. Prices are adjusted for dividends: older prices (and so highs and averages) are lowered for dividends paid, so for a dividend payer they can sit a little below what the chart showed on the day. The 1-year high here and on the Price Data card are the same number. Slow vs fast averages: the trend checks use simple averages, which don't flip on a few noisy days. The price gauge uses a fast (exponential) 21-day average. Stops use neither; they're based on ATR. The price gauge and ladder show where the price sits against its 21, 50 and 200-day averages: the gauge in day-moves, the ladder in real dollars. It follows an old trading idea: buying far above the 21-day average means a farther stop (Livermore's pivotal points, O'Neil's "don't buy extended"). It shows for every stock and only measures; when to buy is your call.
